summary.text: Node encodings can be concatenated, so once a value \(x\) occurs, the legal child values \(2x\) and, when \(x>4\) with \(x\equiv4\pmod 6\), \((x-1)/3\) also occur. Inducting backward along a finite Collatz trajectory ending at \(1\), an even \(m\) is recovered from \(m/2\) by the first move, while for odd \(m\ne1\), the parent \(3m+1\) satisfies the branching condition and the second move recovers \(m\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
B(v)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad v>4\ \text{ and }\ v+2\equiv 0\pmod 6
\]
be the condition that the node of value \(v\) is a branching node (with the exceptional node \(4\) thereby excluded).

It is useful to describe the sequence through a two-variable function \(F(r,v)\): this is the value reached when the path encoded by the nonnegative integer \(r\) is followed starting from a node of value \(v\). Thus \(a(n)=F(n,1)\). The recursive definition is as follows:

* \(F(0,v)=v\).
* If \(r>0\), put \(q=r-1\). If \(B(v)\) holds, then
  \[
  F(r,v)=
  \begin{cases}
  F(q/2,2v),&q\text{ even},\\[2mm]
  F(q/2,(v-1)/3),&q\text{ odd},
  \end{cases}
  \]
  where the divisions are integer divisions.
* If \(r>0\) and \(B(v)\) does not hold, then
  \[
  F(r,v)=F(r-1,2v).
  \]

This is precisely the stated encoding procedure: at a branching node, the parity of the decremented code selects one of the two children and the remaining code is divided by two; at a nonbranching node, the sole child is \(2v\) and the decremented code is retained.

We first prove a concatenation property of this encoding.

**Concatenation lemma.** For all nonnegative integers \(r,v,s\), there is a nonnegative integer \(R\) such that
\[
F(R,v)=F\bigl(s,F(r,v)\bigr).
\]
In words, a path encoded by \(r\), followed by a path encoded by \(s\), can itself be encoded by a single integer \(R\).

We prove this by strong induction on \(r\).

If \(r=0\), then \(F(0,v)=v\), so we may take \(R=s\):
\[
F(R,v)=F(s,v)=F(s,F(0,v)).
\]

Now suppose \(r>0\), put \(q=r-1\), and assume the claim already holds for every first argument smaller than \(r\). Since \(q<r\), and also \(q/2<r\), the induction hypothesis may be used with either of these smaller arguments.

First suppose that \(B(v)\) holds and that \(q\) is even. The first step prescribed by \(r\) goes from \(v\) to \(2v\), leaving the residual code \(q/2\); hence
\[
F(r,v)=F(q/2,2v).
\]
By the induction hypothesis, there is some \(T\) such that
\[
F(T,2v)=F\bigl(s,F(q/2,2v)\bigr).
\]
Take
\[
R=2T+1.
\]
Then \(R-1=2T\) is even and \((R-1)/2=T\). Since the starting node is still the branching node \(v\), the first step in decoding \(R\) chooses the child \(2v\), after which the remaining code is \(T\). Therefore
\[
F(R,v)=F(T,2v)
       =F\bigl(s,F(q/2,2v)\bigr)
       =F(s,F(r,v)).
\]

Next suppose that \(B(v)\) holds and that \(q\) is odd. In this case
\[
F(r,v)=F(q/2,(v-1)/3).
\]
By the induction hypothesis, choose \(T\) such that
\[
F(T,(v-1)/3)
 =F\bigl(s,F(q/2,(v-1)/3)\bigr).
\]
Now take
\[
R=2T+2.
\]
Here \(R-1=2T+1\) is odd and \((R-1)/2=T\). Thus decoding \(R\) at the branching node \(v\) selects the child \((v-1)/3\) and leaves code \(T\). Consequently,
\[
F(R,v)=F(T,(v-1)/3)
       =F\bigl(s,F(q/2,(v-1)/3)\bigr)
       =F(s,F(r,v)).
\]

Finally suppose that \(B(v)\) does not hold. Then the first move is forced, so
\[
F(r,v)=F(q,2v).
\]
By the induction hypothesis there is a \(T\) satisfying
\[
F(T,2v)=F(s,F(q,2v)).
\]
Take \(R=T+1\). Since \(R>0\), its first step from the same nonbranching node \(v\) is the forced move to \(2v\), and the residual code is \(R-1=T\). Hence
\[
F(R,v)=F(T,2v)=F(s,F(q,2v))=F(s,F(r,v)).
\]
This completes the proof of the concatenation lemma.

We next record how to append either kind of inverse-Collatz edge to an already encoded path.

For every \(v\),
\[
F(1,v)=2v.
\]
Indeed, after decrementing the code \(1\), the residual code is \(0\). If \(v\) is nonbranching, the unique move is to \(2v\). If \(v\) is branching, the residual code \(0\) is even, so the same child \(2v\) is selected; in either case there is then no residual path to follow.

Also, whenever \(B(v)\) holds,
\[
F(2,v)=\frac{v-1}{3}.
\]
For after decrementing \(2\), the residual value is \(1\), which is odd, so at the branching node \(v\) the second child \((v-1)/3\) is selected; division of the residual code by two leaves \(0\).

Say that a number \(x\) *appears* if there is an \(r\) such that \(F(r,1)=x\). If \(x\) appears, then \(2x\) appears. To see this, choose \(r\) with \(F(r,1)=x\). Apply the concatenation lemma with starting value \(1\) and appended code \(s=1\). It supplies an \(R\) for which
\[
F(R,1)=F(1,F(r,1))=F(1,x)=2x.
\]
Similarly, if \(x\) appears and \(B(x)\) holds, then \((x-1)/3\) appears. Indeed, append the code \(s=2\); the concatenation lemma gives an \(R\) such that
\[
F(R,1)=F(2,F(r,1))=F(2,x)=\frac{x-1}{3}.
\]

Now define the Collatz map
\[
C(m)=
\begin{cases}
m/2,&m\text{ even},\\
3m+1,&m\text{ odd}.
\end{cases}
\]
We need three elementary observations concerning this map.

First, if \(m>0\), then \(C(m)>0\). If \(m\) is odd, this is immediate from \(C(m)=3m+1\). If \(m\) is even and positive, then \(m\ge 2\), so \(m/2\ge 1\).

Second, if \(m\) is even, then
\[
2C(m)=m,
\]
because \(C(m)=m/2\) and division by two is exact for even \(m\).

Third, suppose \(m>0\) is odd and \(m\ne 1\). Then \(m\ge 3\), and the number
\[
p=C(m)=3m+1
\]
is a branching node. Indeed, \(p=3m+1\ge 10>4\). Moreover, writing the odd number \(m\) as \(m=2t+1\), we get
\[
p+2=3m+3=3(m+1)=3(2t+2)=6(t+1),
\]
so \(p+2\) is divisible by \(6\). Thus \(B(p)\) holds. Furthermore,
\[
\frac{p-1}{3}=\frac{(3m+1)-1}{3}=m.
\]
Therefore the second child of the Collatz-tree node \(p=C(m)\) is exactly \(m\).

We now prove the key assertion:

> If \(m>0\) and \(C^k(m)=1\) for some \(k\ge 0\), then \(m\) appears in the sequence.

Here \(C^k\) denotes the \(k\)-fold iterate of \(C\). We prove the assertion by induction on \(k\).

For \(k=0\), \(C^0(m)=m\), so the hypothesis says \(m=1\). The root itself is represented by code \(0\), since
\[
a(0)=F(0,1)=1=m.
\]
Thus \(m\) appears.

Suppose the assertion is known for \(k\), and assume
\[
C^{k+1}(m)=1
\]
with \(m>0\). If \(m=1\), it again appears at code \(0\). We may therefore assume \(m\ne 1\). Let
\[
p=C(m).
\]
As observed above, \(p>0\), and the equation \(C^{k+1}(m)=1\) is exactly
\[
C^k(p)=1.
\]
The induction hypothesis therefore says that \(p=C(m)\) appears.

There are now two cases.

If \(m\) is even, then \(2p=2C(m)=m\). Since \(p\) appears and appending a halving-type child shows that \(2p\) appears, it follows that \(m\) appears.

If \(m\) is odd, then, because \(m>0\) and \(m\ne1\), the preceding observation shows that \(p=3m+1\) satisfies the branching condition \(B(p)\), and
\[
\frac{p-1}{3}=m.
\]
Since \(p\) appears, appending its tripling-type child shows that \((p-1)/3=m\) appears. This completes the induction.

Finally assume the Collatz conjecture: for every positive integer \(m\), there is a nonnegative integer \(k\) such that \(C^k(m)=1\). Given any \(m>0\), choose such a \(k\). The assertion just proved gives some \(n\ge0\) with
\[
F(n,1)=m.
\]
Since \(a(n)=F(n,1)\), this says \(a(n)=m\). Hence, if the Collatz conjecture is true, every positive integer occurs among the values of A319303.
